push.title: How Vec::push works
push.description: Adds an item at the end; the Vec grows its storage when it is full.

slides.caption: v holds 1 and 2. push(3) puts 3 after the last item.
The existing items stay where they are.
3 is written right after them. If the Vec has no spare room, it first moves everything to a bigger block of memory.
push is fast on average: the Vec reserves extra room when it grows (usually doubling), so most pushes need no move at all.

pop.title: How Vec::pop works
pop.description: Removes the last item and returns it as an Option.

slides.caption: pop removes the last item and gives it back.
3 is the last item: it is taken out.
pop returns Some(3). On an empty Vec it would return None instead of crashing.
push and pop together make a Vec a stack: the last item in is the first item out.

insert.title: How Vec::insert works
insert.description: Puts an item at a position; every later item shifts one place right.

slides.caption: insert(1, 2) needs index 1 free, so everything from index 1 on has to move.
1 is before index 1: it stays.
4 moves one place right first, then 3.
Index 1 is free now, and 2 is written there.
insert near the front of a long Vec is slow, because every later item moves. Inserting at index len() is the same as push.

remove.title: How Vec::remove works
remove.description: Takes the item at an index out; every later item shifts one place left.

slides.caption: remove(1) takes out "b" and closes the gap.
"b" at index 1 is taken out and returned.
"a" stays in place.
"c" and "d" each move one place left to close the gap.
The order is kept, but every later item has to move. When order does not matter, swap_remove is faster.

swap_remove.title: How Vec::swap_remove works
swap_remove.description: Removes an item by moving the last item into its place: fast, but the order changes.

note.text: the last item fills the hole

slides.caption: swap_remove(1) takes out "b", but instead of shifting, it fills the hole with the last item.
"b" is taken out and returned.
"a" and "c" do not move.
"d", the last item, jumps into the hole at index 1.
Only one item moves, however long the Vec is. Use it when you do not care about order.

extend.title: How Vec::extend works
extend.description: Appends every item of an iterator.

slides.caption: extend adds all items of the other collection to the end, in order.
v keeps 1 and 2.
3 and 4 are added after them.
extend works with any iterator, so v.extend(other.iter().filter(...)) is fine too. It reserves room once instead of growing at every push.

append.title: How Vec::append works
append.description: Moves all items of another Vec to the end, leaving the other one empty.

slides.caption: append moves the items out of b and into the end of a.
a keeps its items.
3 is moved from b to the end of a.
Unlike extend, append empties the other Vec instead of copying from it. b still exists and can be reused.

truncate.title: How Vec::truncate works
truncate.description: Keeps the first n items and drops the rest.

slides.caption: truncate(2) keeps items 0 and 1 and drops everything after them.
1 and 2 are kept.
3 and 4 are dropped.
If n is not smaller than the length, truncate does nothing. The capacity stays the same.

retain.title: How Vec::retain works
retain.description: Keeps only the items for which the closure returns true, in place.

title.text: let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4]; v.retain(|x| x % 2 == 0);

slides.caption: retain checks every item and removes the ones that fail, keeping the order of the rest.
1 is odd: removed.
2 is even: kept.
3 is odd: removed.
4 is even: kept.
retain changes the Vec itself. To keep the original, use iter().filter(...).collect() instead.

dedup.title: How Vec::dedup works
dedup.description: Removes repeated items that sit next to each other.

slides.caption: dedup compares each item with the one before it and removes it if they are equal.
The first 1 is kept.
The second 1 equals its neighbour: removed.
2 differs from 1: kept.
The last 1 differs from its neighbour 2, so it stays, even though there was a 1 before.
To remove all duplicates, sort first: v.sort(); v.dedup(); gives [1, 2].

dedup_by_key.title: How Vec::dedup_by_key works
dedup_by_key.description: Removes neighbours whose computed keys are equal.

slides.caption: dedup_by_key compares keys (here x / 10) instead of the items themselves.
10 has key 1: kept.
11 also has key 1, like its neighbour: removed.
20 has key 2: kept. 21 has key 2 too: removed.
30 has key 3: kept.
The first item of each run of equal keys is kept.

drain.title: How Vec::drain works
drain.description: Removes a range of items and gives them back as an iterator.

title.text: let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4]; let taken: Vec<_> = v.drain(1..3).collect();

slides.caption: drain(1..3) cuts out the items at index 1 and 2.
2 and 3 are in the range 1..3: they are taken out.
1 and 4 remain in v, and the gap is closed.
drain(..) empties the whole Vec but keeps its memory, which is handy for reusing a buffer.

split_off.title: How Vec::split_off works
split_off.description: Cuts the Vec in two at an index and returns the second part.

title.text: let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4]; let tail = v.split_off(1);

slides.caption: split_off(1) moves the items from index 1 to the end into a new Vec.
1 stays in v.
2, 3 and 4 move to the new Vec, which split_off returns.
split_off(0) moves everything; split_off(len) returns an empty Vec. An index past the end panics.

resize.title: How Vec::resize works
resize.description: Makes the Vec exactly n long: pads with a value or cuts off the end.

slides.caption: resize(4, 0) wants 4 items. v has 2, so two copies of 0 are added.
The existing items stay.
Copies of 0 are pushed until the length is 4.
With a smaller length, resize works like truncate: v.resize(1, 0) gives [1].

clear.title: How Vec::clear works
clear.description: Removes every item but keeps the allocated memory.

slides.caption: clear drops all items at once.
All three items are dropped.
The memory is kept, so pushing new items later needs no new allocation.
clear is the cheap way to reuse a Vec in a loop. To give the memory back too, follow it with shrink_to_fit().

len.title: How Vec::len works
len.description: The number of items in the Vec.

slides.caption: A Vec always knows how many items it holds.
There are three items, at indexes 0, 1 and 2.
len() returns 3 without counting: the number is stored next to the items.
The last valid index is len() - 1. Use is_empty() rather than len() == 0.

with_capacity.title: How Vec::with_capacity works
with_capacity.description: Creates an empty Vec with room reserved for n items.

title.text: let mut v = Vec::with_capacity(4); v.push(1); v.push(2);

slides.caption: with_capacity(4) reserves room for 4 items up front. The Vec is still empty: its length is 0.
push(1) and push(2) use two of the reserved places. No allocation happens.
Two places are still free, so the next two pushes are free too.
If you know roughly how many items are coming, with_capacity avoids repeated moves while the Vec grows.

extend_from_slice.title: How Vec::extend_from_slice works
extend_from_slice.description: Appends clones of every item in a slice.

note.text: the slice itself is not changed

slides.caption: extend_from_slice copies the items of the slice to the end of v.
v starts with 1.
2 and 3 are copied in. The slice still has them too.
Use it with a slice of Clone items; for any iterator, use extend.

into_iter.title: How Vec::into_iter works
into_iter.description: Turns the Vec into an iterator of owned items: the Vec is used up.

title.text: for s in v { ... }   // v = vec![String::from("a"), String::from("b")]

slides.caption: for s in v calls v.into_iter(). Each item is moved out of the Vec, so s owns it.
"a" is moved out of v into s.
"b" is moved out too.
After the loop v no longer exists: using it would be a compile error ("value moved").
Write for s in &v to only borrow the items (s is &String) and keep v usable afterwards.

is_empty.title: How Vec::is_empty works
is_empty.description: true when the Vec has no items.

slides.caption: is_empty checks whether the length is 0.
An empty Vec: true.
A Vec with one item: false.
Clippy suggests is_empty() over len() == 0 because it reads better.

retain_mut.title: How Vec::retain_mut works
retain_mut.description: Like retain, but the closure may also change the items it keeps.

slides.caption: Each item is decreased by one; items that reach 0 are removed.
1 becomes 0: not > 0, removed.
3 becomes 2: kept.
2 becomes 1: kept.
Handy for timers and lifetimes: tick everything down and drop what has expired, in one pass.

reserve.title: How Vec::reserve works
reserve.description: Makes sure there is room for at least n more items.

slides.caption: reserve(10) grows the buffer so that 10 more pushes will not need to reallocate.
v holds one item.
After reserve(10), the capacity is at least 1 + 10. The length is still 1.
reserve may give more than asked for, never less. Use it before a loop of pushes when you know how many are coming.
